solution:
Apply the chapter's rules: the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is zero (and equals the charge in an ion); \(\text{Na}\) is \(+1\), \(\text{K}\) is \(+1\), \(\text{Ca}\) is \(+2\), \(\text{Al}\) is \(+3\); \(\text{H}\) is \(+1\) and \(\text{O}\) is \(-2\) except in the peroxides, where each \(\text{O}\) is \(-1\).
(a) \(\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4\): \((+1) + 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5\).
(b) \(\text{NaHSO}_4\): \((+1) + (+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\).
(c) \(\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_7\): \(4(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 2x = 10 \Rightarrow x = +5\).
(d) \(\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4\): \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\).
(e) \(\text{CaO}_2\) is calcium PEROXIDE. Calcium is an alkaline earth metal and is fixed at \(+2\), so the two oxygens must share \(-2\) between them: \((+2) + 2x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1\). This is the peroxide exception to the \(\text{O} = -2\) rule, not an ordinary oxide.
(f) \(\text{NaBH}_4\): the chapter's rule 4 makes hydrogen \(-1\) only in BINARY metal hydrides, which this is not, so the rule as worded does not settle it. Fall back on the principle the rules are built from — the shared pair belongs to the more electronegative atom. Hydrogen is more electronegative than boron, so each \(\text{H}\) here is \(-1\): \((+1) + x + 4(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +3\). (Taking \(\text{H} = +1\) would give \(x = -5\), impossible for a group-13 element.)
(g) \(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7\): \(2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 2x = 12 \Rightarrow x = +6\).
(h) \(\text{KAl(SO}_4)_2 \cdot 12\text{H}_2\text{O}\): the water of crystallisation is neutral and \(\text{K} = +1\), \(\text{Al} = +3\), so each sulphate carries \(-2\). Within \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\): \(x + 4(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6\).
Answers: (a) P \(+5\)  (b) S \(+6\)  (c) P \(+5\)  (d) Mn \(+6\)  (e) O \(-1\)  (f) B \(+3\)  (g) S \(+6\)  (h) S \(+6\).

Each of these gives a FRACTIONAL value, and the chapter's own discussion of fractional oxidation numbers supplies the rationalisation: the algebraic rule returns an AVERAGE, while the structure shows the atoms of that element are actually in different whole-number states.
(a) \(\text{KI}_3\): \((+1) + 3x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\tfrac{1}{3}\). Structurally the triiodide is \(\text{K}^{+}[\text{I}\!-\!\text{I}\!-\!\text{I}]^{-}\), i.e. an iodide ion holding a neutral \(\text{I}_2\) molecule — two iodines at \(0\) and one at \(-1\), averaging \(-\tfrac{1}{3}\).
(b) \(\text{H}_2\text{S}_4\text{O}_6\): \(2(+1) + 4x + 6(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 4x = 10 \Rightarrow x = +2.5\). The chapter gives the structure of the tetrathionate ion \(\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}\): the two terminal sulphurs are \(+5\) and the two middle, mutually bonded sulphurs are \(0\); the average of \(+5, 0, 0, +5\) is \(+2.5\).
(c) \(\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4\): \(3x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +\tfrac{8}{3}\). It is a MIXED oxide, \(\text{FeO} \cdot \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\) — one \(\text{Fe(II)}\) and two \(\text{Fe(III)}\), averaging \((2+3+3)/3 = \tfrac{8}{3}\).
(d) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\): assign each carbon separately, counting \(-1\) for every bond to the less electronegative hydrogen, \(+1\) for every bond to the more electronegative oxygen and \(0\) for the C\(-\)C bond. The methyl carbon has three C\(-\)H bonds, so it is \(-3\); the carbinol carbon has two C\(-\)H and one C\(-\)O, so it is \(-2 + 1 = -1\). (The algebraic rule on the whole molecule returns their average, \(-2\).)
(e) \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\): the methyl carbon again has three C\(-\)H bonds and is \(-3\); the carboxyl carbon is doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly to another, giving \(+2 + 1 = +3\). (Their average is \(0\), which is what the algebraic rule returns.)
Answers: (a) \(-\tfrac{1}{3}\)  (b) \(+2.5\)  (c) \(+\tfrac{8}{3}\)  (d) \(-3\) for the methyl carbon and \(-1\) for the carbinol carbon  (e) \(-3\) for the methyl carbon and \(+3\) for the carboxyl carbon. In every case the fraction is only an average and does not describe any single atom.

[Textbook error in the QUESTION'S OWN PREMISE, for part (c). The instruction is "justify that the following reactions ARE redox reactions", but in \(4\text{BCl}_3 + 3\text{LiAlH}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 3\text{LiCl} + 3\text{AlCl}_3\) NO element changes its oxidation number: boron is \(+3\) on both sides, hydrogen \(-1\) on both sides, and lithium, chlorine and aluminium are unchanged. It is a metathesis (a ligand exchange of hydride for chloride), not a redox reaction. THE READING TURNS ENTIRELY ON HYDROGEN, so both are set out below and the reader should know which they are being asked for. Hydrogen (electronegativity 2.20) is MORE electronegative than both boron (2.04) and aluminium (1.61), so in \(\text{LiAlH}_4\) and in \(\text{B}_2\text{H}_6\) it is \(-1\) and boron stays \(+3\) — that is the analysis below, and it follows the principle the chapter's rules are derived from. Applied LITERALLY, however, the chapter's rule 4 says hydrogen is \(+1\) except in metal hydrides; boron is a metalloid rather than a metal, so a strict reading gives \(\text{H} = +1\) and \(\text{B} = -3\) in \(\text{B}_2\text{H}_6\), which WOULD make the reaction redox, and that is what most answer guides print. **This exercise carries no entry in the printed answer key, so nothing external settles it.** Parts (a), (b), (d) and (e) are genuine redox reactions and are unaffected.] A reaction is redox if some element's oxidation number rises while another's falls.
(a) \(\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\): copper falls \(+2 \rightarrow 0\) (reduced) and hydrogen rises \(0 \rightarrow +1\) (oxidised). On the classical definition, oxygen is removed from \(\text{CuO}\) and added to \(\text{H}_2\). Redox.
(b) \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{CO} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_2\): iron falls \(+3 \rightarrow 0\), carbon rises \(+2 \rightarrow +4\). Redox.
(d) \(2\text{K} + \text{F}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{K}^{+}\text{F}^{-}\): potassium rises \(0 \rightarrow +1\) by losing an electron, fluorine falls \(0 \rightarrow -1\) by gaining one. The half reactions are \(2\text{K} \rightarrow 2\text{K}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-}\) and \(\text{F}_2 + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{F}^{-}\). Redox.
(e) \(4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\): nitrogen rises \(-3 \rightarrow +2\), oxygen falls \(0 \rightarrow -2\). Redox.
(c) \(4\text{BCl}_3 + 3\text{LiAlH}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 3\text{LiCl} + 3\text{AlCl}_3\) does NOT fit the pattern. Assigning oxidation numbers by the chapter's rules: in \(\text{BCl}_3\), \(\text{Cl} = -1\) and \(\text{B} = +3\); in \(\text{LiAlH}_4\), \(\text{Li} = +1\), \(\text{Al} = +3\) and \(\text{H} = -1\) (hydrogen is more electronegative than aluminium); in \(\text{B}_2\text{H}_6\), hydrogen is likewise more electronegative than boron so \(\text{H} = -1\) and \(\text{B} = +3\); in \(\text{LiCl}\), \(\text{Li} = +1\), \(\text{Cl} = -1\); in \(\text{AlCl}_3\), \(\text{Al} = +3\), \(\text{Cl} = -1\). Every element therefore keeps the state it started in — \(\text{B}\) stays \(+3\), \(\text{Al}\) stays \(+3\), \(\text{Li}\) stays \(+1\), \(\text{H}\) stays \(-1\), \(\text{Cl}\) stays \(-1\). No oxidation number changes, so on the chapter's own criterion this is not a redox reaction at all but a double-displacement (metathesis) in which hydride and chloride simply exchange partners.
Answer: (a), (b), (d) and (e) are redox reactions, for the oxidation-number changes shown; (c) is not, because no element in it changes oxidation number.
_note:
Part (c) is a genuine problem with the question as set. The chapter asks the student to 'justify that the following reactions are redox reactions', but applying the chapter's own oxidation-number rules to 4BCl3 + 3LiAlH4 -> 2B2H6 + 3LiCl + 3AlCl3 leaves every element unchanged (B +3, Al +3, Li +1, H -1, Cl -1 on both sides), because hydrogen is more electronegative than BOTH boron and aluminium and so is -1 in the hydride and in diborane alike. The solution says so rather than manufacturing a change. If the printed key claims a change here, that is a disagreement worth adjudicating, not an error on our side. NOTE: this row is NOT keyed (only 7.25 is), so nothing external will ever settle it.

THE RUNNER-UP READING, named so the maintainer can adjudicate rather than re-derive: apply p-05's rule 4 LITERALLY — 'hydrogen is +1 except when bonded to metals in binary compounds' — and since boron is not a metal, H would be +1 in B2H6, giving B reduced +3 -> -3 and H oxidised -1 -> +1, i.e. a redox reaction after all, which is what the question's premise asserts. Two things argue against it. First, rule 4 as worded settles NEITHER compound (LiAlH4 is not binary either), so it cannot be the governing rule here; what does govern is the principle the rules are derived from and which the chapter states on p-04/05 — the bonding pair belongs to the more electronegative element — and H (2.20) is more electronegative than both B (2.04) and Al (1.61). Second, hydrogen being -1 in LiAlH4 is FORCED independently by rule 2 (all aluminium is +3), so the left-hand side is not in doubt; only B2H6 is, and treating the same element by two different conventions on the two sides of one equation is what manufactures the change. Worth knowing: the 24-electron balance under the runner-up reading is NOT independent evidence for it, because flipping the sign convention on the same twelve hydrogens must balance by construction.

solution:
Assign oxidation numbers to every element on both sides.
In \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\): \(\text{H} = +1\), \(\text{O} = -2\). In \(\text{F}_2\): \(\text{F} = 0\) (free element). In \(\text{HF}\): \(\text{H} = +1\), \(\text{F} = -1\). In \(\text{HOF}\): fluorine is the most electronegative element and by the chapter's rule 5 is always \(-1\); hydrogen is \(+1\); so oxygen must be \((+1) + x + (-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0\).
So two changes occur simultaneously:
Fluorine: \(0 \rightarrow -1\) in both \(\text{HF}\) and \(\text{HOF}\) — fluorine is REDUCED, and \(\text{F}_2\) is the oxidising agent.
Oxygen: \(-2 \rightarrow 0\) in \(\text{HOF}\) — oxygen is OXIDISED, and water is the reducing agent.
The electron bookkeeping balances: the two fluorine atoms gain one electron each (\(2\text{e}^{-}\) in all) while the one oxygen atom loses two.
Since the oxidation number of one element increases while that of another decreases in the same reaction, this is a redox reaction. It is also a rare one: oxygen is normally the element doing the oxidising, and it can be oxidised here only because fluorine is the single element more electronegative than oxygen.

First apply the rules mechanically, taking every oxygen as \(-2\).
\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_5\): \(2(+1) + x + 5(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +8\).
\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\): \(2x + 7(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow 2x = 12 \Rightarrow x = +6\).
\(\text{NO}_3^{-}\): \(x + 3(-2) = -1 \Rightarrow x = +5\).
Now test each against the maximum the element can reach. The chapter's rule is that the highest oxidation number of a representative element is its group number for groups 1 and 2 and the group number minus 10 for the rest. Sulphur is in group 16, so its maximum is \(+6\); nitrogen is in group 15, so its maximum is \(+5\); chromium's group number is 6, so its maximum is \(+6\).
THE FALLACY IS IN \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_5\) ALONE. A value of \(+8\) for sulphur is impossible — sulphur has only six valence electrons to lose. The error is in the assumption, not the arithmetic: peroxomonosulphuric acid (Caro's acid) contains a PEROXIDE linkage, and the chapter states explicitly that in a peroxide each oxygen is \(-1\), not \(-2\). Its structure is \(\text{HO}\!-\!\text{SO}_2\!-\!\text{O}\!-\!\text{OH}\): sulphur is bonded to two doubly bonded oxygens and one hydroxyl, all at \(-2\), plus a peroxo \(-\text{O}\!-\!\text{O}-\) pair at \(-1\) each. Recomputing, \(2(+1) + x + 3(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\), which is within sulphur's limit.
The other two carry no fallacy. \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\) is two \(\text{CrO}_4\) tetrahedra joined through a single BRIDGING oxygen, \(\text{O}_3\text{Cr}\!-\!\text{O}\!-\!\text{CrO}_3\); every oxygen is \(-2\) and there is no O\(-\)O bond, so \(+6\) stands and is exactly chromium's maximum. \(\text{NO}_3^{-}\) is planar with the nitrogen at the centre of three equivalent oxygens (the negative charge delocalised over them); again every oxygen is \(-2\) and \(+5\) stands, which is nitrogen's maximum.
Answers: S \(= +6\) (not the \(+8\) the naive calculation gives, because of the peroxide linkage), Cr \(= +6\), N \(= +5\).

In Stock notation the Roman numeral after the metal IS its oxidation number, so read the numeral, pair it with the charge on the anion and take the lowest whole-number ratio that makes the formula electrically neutral. The anions are chloride \(\text{Cl}^{-}\), sulphate \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) and oxide \(\text{O}^{2-}\).
(a) Mercury(II) chloride: \(\text{Hg}^{2+}\) with two \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) — \(\text{HgCl}_2\).
(b) Nickel(II) sulphate: \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) with one \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) — \(\text{NiSO}_4\).
(c) Tin(IV) oxide: \(\text{Sn}^{4+}\) with two \(\text{O}^{2-}\) — \(\text{SnO}_2\).
(d) Thallium(I) sulphate: two \(\text{Tl}^{+}\) with one \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) — \(\text{Tl}_2\text{SO}_4\).
(e) Iron(III) sulphate: two \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) with three \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) — \(\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\).
(f) Chromium(III) oxide: two \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) with three \(\text{O}^{2-}\) — \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3\).
Answers: (a) \(\text{HgCl}_2\)  (b) \(\text{NiSO}_4\)  (c) \(\text{SnO}_2\)  (d) \(\text{Tl}_2\text{SO}_4\)  (e) \(\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\)  (f) \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3\).

Count each bond from the atom in question: \(-1\) for every bond to a less electronegative atom (hydrogen), \(+1\) for every bond to a more electronegative one (oxygen, chlorine), and \(0\) for a bond to a like atom.
CARBON, from \(-4\) to \(+4\):
\(-4\): \(\text{CH}_4\) (four C\(-\)H bonds)
\(-3\): \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) (each carbon has three C\(-\)H and one C\(-\)C)
\(-2\): \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\) (three C\(-\)H, one C\(-\)Cl), or \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)
\(-1\): \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\) (each carbon has one C\(-\)H and a C\(\equiv\)C)
\(0\): \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\), or \(\text{HCHO}\)
\(+1\): \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\), glyoxal \(\text{OHC}\!-\!\text{CHO}\) (each carbon: one C\(-\)H, one C\(=\)O, one C\(-\)C)
\(+2\): \(\text{CHCl}_3\), or \(\text{CO}\)
\(+3\): \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4\), oxalic acid (each carbon: one C\(=\)O, one C\(-\)OH, one C\(-\)C)
\(+4\): \(\text{CCl}_4\), or \(\text{CO}_2\)
NITROGEN, from \(-3\) to \(+5\):
\(-3\): \(\text{NH}_3\)
\(-2\): \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\) (hydrazine)
\(-1\): \(\text{NH}_2\text{OH}\) (hydroxylamine)
\(0\): \(\text{N}_2\)
\(+1\): \(\text{N}_2\text{O}\)
\(+2\): \(\text{NO}\)
\(+3\): \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_3\) or \(\text{HNO}_2\)
\(+4\): \(\text{NO}_2\) (or \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\))
\(+5\): \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\) or \(\text{HNO}_3\)
Note that the two limits are exactly what the chapter's group rule predicts: carbon is in group 14, so it runs from \(14 - 10 = +4\) down to \(-4\); nitrogen is in group 15, so it runs from \(15 - 10 = +5\) down to \(-3\).

A substance can act as a REDUCING agent only if the key element in it can be pushed to a HIGHER oxidation state, and as an OXIDISING agent only if that element can drop to a LOWER one. So the question is simply whether the element is in an intermediate state or already at an extreme.
\(\text{SO}_2\): sulphur is \(+4\). Sulphur's range runs from \(-2\) to \(+6\), so \(+4\) is INTERMEDIATE. It can rise to \(+6\) (as in \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\)), in which case \(\text{SO}_2\) has acted as a reductant, or fall towards \(0\) or \(-2\) (as in \(\text{S}\) or \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\)), in which case it has acted as an oxidant. Hence both.
\(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\): oxygen is \(-1\), midway between \(0\) in \(\text{O}_2\) and \(-2\) in \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\). It can be oxidised to \(\text{O}_2\) (acting as a reductant) or reduced to \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) (acting as an oxidant). Indeed it does BOTH to itself, in the disproportionation \(2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2\) the chapter gives.
\(\text{O}_3\): oxygen is at \(0\), and since oxygen is second only to fluorine in electronegativity, \(0\) is effectively the HIGHEST state it reaches in ordinary compounds. There is nowhere further up to go, so ozone can only take electrons — it acts only as an oxidant.
\(\text{HNO}_3\): nitrogen is at \(+5\), which is its MAXIMUM (group 15, so \(15 - 10 = +5\)); all five valence electrons are already accounted for. Nitrogen cannot be oxidised further, so nitric acid can only be reduced and acts only as an oxidant.
Answer: \(\text{SO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\) act both ways because their key element sits in an intermediate oxidation state; \(\text{O}_3\) and \(\text{HNO}_3\) act only as oxidants because their key element is already in its highest attainable oxidation state.

In both cases the shorter equation is correctly balanced but hides WHICH reactant the product oxygen came from, and that is precisely the redox information.
(a) Written as \(6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2\), nothing says whether the dioxygen released comes from the carbon dioxide or from the water. Writing \(6\text{CO}_2 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + 6\text{O}_2\) shows twelve water molecules consumed and six regenerated, which makes explicit that ALL twelve oxygen atoms of the evolved \(\text{O}_2\) come from WATER. Water is therefore the reducing agent (its oxygen rises \(-2 \rightarrow 0\)) and carbon dioxide the oxidising agent (its carbon falls \(+4\) to an average of \(0\) in glucose).
(b) Written as \(\text{O}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{O}_2\), the two dioxygen molecules look interchangeable. Writing \(\text{O}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2 + \text{O}_2\) shows that they are not: ONE comes from the ozone and the OTHER from the hydrogen peroxide. Here hydrogen peroxide is the reductant (its oxygen rises \(-1 \rightarrow 0\)) and ozone the oxidant (one of its oxygens falls \(0 \rightarrow -2\) in the water).
Technique to investigate the path: ISOTOPIC LABELLING followed by mass spectrometry. Repeat each reaction with one reactant enriched in the heavy oxygen isotope \(^{18}\text{O}\) — labelled water in (a), labelled hydrogen peroxide in (b) — and then analyse the dioxygen evolved. If the label turns up in the \(\text{O}_2\), that reactant was its source; if the \(\text{O}_2\) comes back unlabelled, it was not. The experiment tells the two proposed paths apart in a way the balanced equation alone cannot.
Answer: the longer forms are more appropriate because they identify water (in a) and hydrogen peroxide (in b) as the actual sources of the evolved dioxygen, and hence as the reducing agents; isotopic labelling with \(^{18}\text{O}\) confirms it experimentally.
_note: The isotopic-labelling technique is not developed anywhere in this chapter — the chapter stops at classifying and balancing redox reactions. It is supplied because the question explicitly asks for a technique, and it is named as the standard method rather than derived from the chapter's own material.

solution:
Fluorine is always \(-1\) (the chapter's rule 5), so in \(\text{AgF}_2\) the silver must be \(x + 2(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +2\).
Silver's normal and stable oxidation state is \(+1\); \(\text{Ag(II)}\) is an abnormally high state for it, which is why the compound is unstable. An element held in an unusually high oxidation state has a strong tendency to fall back to its stable one, and falling to a lower oxidation state means ACCEPTING electrons — which is the definition of an oxidising agent.
So if \(\text{AgF}_2\) is formed at all, the \(\text{Ag}^{2+}\) in it seizes an electron from almost anything available:
\(\text{Ag}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}^{+}\)
and the driving force for that step — the same instability that makes the compound hard to prepare — is what makes it a very powerful oxidant.
Answer: because silver is forced into the \(+2\) state in \(\text{AgF}_2\), well above its stable \(+1\), and reverts to \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) by taking an electron from any species it meets.

The reagent present in excess drives its partner as far along the oxidation-number scale as that partner can go. If the reducing agent is in excess, the oxidising agent is pushed all the way DOWN to its lowest accessible state; if the oxidising agent is in excess, the reducing agent is pushed all the way UP.
Illustration 1 — phosphorus with chlorine. With phosphorus in excess (chlorine limited), phosphorus stops at \(+3\):
\(\text{P}_4 + 6\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{PCl}_3\)
With chlorine in excess it is taken to \(+5\):
\(\text{P}_4 + 10\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{PCl}_5\)
Illustration 2 — carbon with dioxygen. With carbon in excess (the reducing agent in excess), carbon reaches only \(+2\):
\(2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}\)
With dioxygen in excess it reaches its maximum \(+4\):
\(\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\)
Illustration 3 — hydrogen sulphide with dioxygen. With \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) in excess (limited oxygen), sulphur is oxidised only to \(0\):
\(2\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
With dioxygen in excess it goes on to \(+4\):
\(2\text{H}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
A fourth, on the other side of the statement, is sodium with dioxygen: with the metal in excess the oxygen is taken right down to \(-2\), \(4\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}\), whereas with dioxygen in excess it stops at \(-1\) as the peroxide, \(2\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O}_2\).
In every pair the stoichiometry is the only thing that changed, and it changed the oxidation state of the product — which is exactly what the statement claims.

(a) All three permanganate reagents oxidise the methyl group of toluene to a carboxyl group, but the aqueous ones are in a DIFFERENT PHASE from the toluene: toluene is a non-polar liquid essentially insoluble in water, so with aqueous alkaline or acidic \(\text{KMnO}_4\) the two reactants meet only at the interface between two layers and the oxidation is slow and incomplete. Alcohol dissolves BOTH the potassium permanganate and the toluene, so an alcoholic solution brings them into a single homogeneous phase where the reaction proceeds smoothly and can be stopped cleanly at benzoic acid.
A balanced equation for the oxidation is
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{KMnO}_4 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOK} + 2\text{MnO}_2 + \text{KOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
followed by acidification of the salt,
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOK} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{KCl}\)
The electron bookkeeping checks: the methyl carbon rises from \(-3\) to \(+3\), losing six electrons, while each of the two manganese atoms falls from \(+7\) to \(+4\), gaining three — six in all.
(b) Concentrated sulphuric acid is not only an acid but also an oxidising agent, since its sulphur is at \(+6\). With a chloride it acts only as an acid, displacing the more volatile hydrogen chloride:
\(\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}\)
It cannot oxidise \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) to \(\text{Cl}_2\), because chloride is a poor reducing agent — chlorine itself is a strong oxidant, so the electron is held tightly.
Bromide is a distinctly BETTER reducing agent than chloride. The chapter states that the oxidising power of the halogens falls from fluorine to iodine, which is the same fact seen from the other side: the halide ion gives up its electron more readily as the group is descended. Concentrated sulphuric acid is therefore strong enough to oxidise \(\text{Br}^{-}\), and free bromine appears as a red vapour while the sulphur is reduced from \(+6\) to \(+4\):
\(2\text{KBr} + 3\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{KHSO}_4 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{Br}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Answer: (a) because alcohol dissolves both reactants and so provides the homogeneous medium the aqueous reagents cannot; (b) because \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) is too weak a reductant to be oxidised by \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) (so only HCl is displaced) whereas \(\text{Br}^{-}\) is strong enough to be oxidised to \(\text{Br}_2\).
_note: The reason in (a) — solvent miscibility — is standard organic-chemistry practice and is NOT discussed anywhere in this chapter, which never mentions toluene, benzoic acid or alcoholic permanganate. It is given because the question asks for it, and is flagged here as coming from outside the chapter.

solution:
In each case find the element whose oxidation number rises (that species is oxidised and is the reducing agent) and the element whose oxidation number falls (that species is reduced and is the oxidising agent).
(a) Silver falls \(+1 \rightarrow 0\). The carbon of hydroquinone \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\) rises from an average \(-\tfrac{1}{3}\) to \(0\) in quinone \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\) — equivalently, two hydrogens are removed, which is oxidation on the classical definition.
Oxidised: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\).  Reduced: \(\text{AgBr}\).  Oxidising agent: \(\text{AgBr}\).  Reducing agent: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\).
(b) Silver falls \(+1 \rightarrow 0\). The carbon of \(\text{HCHO}\) rises \(0 \rightarrow +2\) in \(\text{HCOO}^{-}\).
Oxidised: \(\text{HCHO}\).  Reduced: \([\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^{+}\).  Oxidising agent: \([\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^{+}\).  Reducing agent: \(\text{HCHO}\).
(c) Copper falls \(+2 \rightarrow +1\) in \(\text{Cu}_2\text{O}\); the carbon of \(\text{HCHO}\) again rises \(0 \rightarrow +2\).
Oxidised: \(\text{HCHO}\).  Reduced: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\).  Oxidising agent: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\).  Reducing agent: \(\text{HCHO}\).
(d) Nitrogen rises \(-2\) in \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\) to \(0\) in \(\text{N}_2\); the oxygen of the peroxide falls \(-1 \rightarrow -2\) in water.
Oxidised: \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\).  Reduced: \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\).  Oxidising agent: \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\).  Reducing agent: \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\).
(e) Both changes are in lead, from its two different starting states: the free metal rises \(0 \rightarrow +2\) while the lead of \(\text{PbO}_2\) falls \(+4 \rightarrow +2\), both ending as \(\text{PbSO}_4\). (This is the discharge reaction of the lead storage battery.)
Oxidised: \(\text{Pb}\).  Reduced: \(\text{PbO}_2\).  Oxidising agent: \(\text{PbO}_2\).  Reducing agent: \(\text{Pb}\).

The difference is one of oxidising STRENGTH, and it shows up as a difference in how far the same reductant is driven.
In thiosulphate \(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}\), sulphur averages \(2x + 3(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +2\).
With iodine the product is tetrathionate, \(\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}\), in which sulphur averages \(4x + 6(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +2.5\). So the sulphur rises only from \(+2\) to \(+2.5\) — a loss of just one electron per thiosulphate ion, which is simply the joining of two thiosulphate ions through an S\(-\)S bond.
With bromine the product is sulphate, \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\), in which sulphur is \(+6\) — its MAXIMUM. Here each sulphur rises from \(+2\) to \(+6\), so eight electrons are lost per thiosulphate ion.
Why the two oxidants stop at different points is given by their standard electrode potentials in the chapter's own Table 7.1: \(\text{I}_2/\text{I}^{-}\) is \(0.54\,\text{V}\) whereas \(\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^{-}\) is \(1.09\,\text{V}\). Iodine is a comparatively MILD oxidising agent and can take the thiosulphate only as far as tetrathionate; bromine is a much STRONGER one and oxidises the sulphur all the way to sulphate.
Answer: thiosulphate reacts differently because bromine is a far stronger oxidant than iodine, and a stronger oxidant drives the same reducing agent to a higher oxidation state — \(+6\) (sulphate) with bromine against only \(+2.5\) (tetrathionate) with iodine. This is the same principle the previous exercise states about excess oxidant.

FLUORINE IS THE BEST OXIDANT AMONG THE HALOGENS. The chapter states that the power of the halogens as oxidising agents decreases on going down group 17, and Table 7.1 puts numbers on it: \(\text{F}_2/\text{F}^{-} = 2.87\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^{-} = 1.36\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^{-} = 1.09\,\text{V}\), \(\text{I}_2/\text{I}^{-} = 0.54\,\text{V}\). The displacement reactions show it directly, each halogen displacing every halide below it and none above:
\(\text{F}_2 + 2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{F}^{-} + \text{Cl}_2\)
\(\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{KBr} \rightarrow 2\text{KCl} + \text{Br}_2\)
\(\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{KI} \rightarrow 2\text{KCl} + \text{I}_2\)
\(\text{Br}_2 + 2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^{-} + \text{I}_2\)
Iodine displaces none of the others. Fluorine sits at the top and is so powerful that it is not even stopped by water — it oxidises the oxygen of water itself, which no other halogen does:
\(2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{F}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{HF} + \text{O}_2\)
HYDROIODIC ACID IS THE BEST REDUCTANT AMONG THE HYDROHALIC ACIDS. Reducing power runs opposite to oxidising power, so the halide ions rank \(\text{I}^{-} > \text{Br}^{-} > \text{Cl}^{-} > \text{F}^{-}\): the least positive potential, \(0.54\,\text{V}\) for \(\text{I}_2/\text{I}^{-}\), means iodide parts with its electron most readily. At the other end, the chapter says there is NO way to convert \(\text{F}^{-}\) to \(\text{F}_2\) by chemical means at all, so \(\text{HF}\) is the poorest reductant of the four.
This is why concentrated sulphuric acid is reduced further and further along the series:
\(8\text{HI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 4\text{I}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{S} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\)  (sulphur taken from \(+6\) right down to \(-2\))
\(2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)  (only to \(+4\))
while \(\text{HCl}\) and \(\text{HF}\) do not reduce it at all.
Answer: fluorine is the best oxidant because it has the highest standard electrode potential of the halogens and displaces every other halide (and even oxidises water), while hydroiodic acid is the best reductant because iodide has the lowest potential of the halides and gives up its electron most easily, reducing sulphuric acid all the way to \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\).

Assign oxidation numbers. In \(\text{XeO}_6^{4-}\): \(x + 6(-2) = -4 \Rightarrow x = +8\). In \(\text{XeO}_3\): \(x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\). Fluorine goes from \(-1\) in \(\text{F}^{-}\) to \(0\) in \(\text{F}_2\).
So xenon is REDUCED from \(+8\) to \(+6\) and fluoride is OXIDISED from \(-1\) to \(0\).
Why the reaction occurs is the striking part. The chapter states that fluoride is the poorest reducing agent there is — that there is no way at all to convert \(\text{F}^{-}\) to \(\text{F}_2\) by chemical means, and that the only route is electrolytic oxidation. Any reagent that nevertheless succeeds in taking an electron from \(\text{F}^{-}\) must therefore be an oxidising agent stronger than fluorine itself. \(\text{XeO}_6^{4-}\) does exactly that, so it is such a reagent. The driving force is that xenon in \(\text{XeO}_6^{4-}\) is in its MAXIMUM oxidation state \(+8\) (group 18, so \(18 - 10 = +8\)) and falls readily to the more stable \(+6\).
Conclusion about \(\text{Na}_4\text{XeO}_6\): it is an extraordinarily powerful oxidising agent — stronger even than fluorine, and therefore among the strongest oxidants known — because it holds xenon at its highest attainable oxidation state.
Answer: the reaction occurs because \(\text{XeO}_6^{4-}\) (xenon at \(+8\)) is a stronger oxidant than \(\text{F}_2\) and so can oxidise even fluoride ion; hence \(\text{Na}_4\text{XeO}_6\) is a very strong oxidising agent.

[Textbook misprint in part (b): the equation does not balance in sulphur. Two \(\text{CuSO}_4\) on the left carry two sulphur atoms, while the single \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) printed on the right carries one. The coefficient should be \(2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\), which balances hydrogen at the same time — left \(3 + 4 = 7\), right \(3 + 4 = 7\) — so one correction closes both. The reaction the question asks about is otherwise as printed, and the answer below uses the balanced form.] Compare which reductant each metal ion is able to take electrons from.
Hypophosphorous acid \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2\) is a strong reducing agent — its phosphorus rises from \(+1\) to \(+5\) in \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\), a loss of four electrons — and it reduces BOTH metal ions to the free metal: \(\text{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Ag}\) in the first reaction and \(\text{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Cu}\) in the second.
Benzaldehyde is a much MILDER reducing agent (its carbonyl carbon rises only from \(+1\) to \(+3\) in the benzoate ion, a loss of two electrons). It reduces \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) to metallic silver in the third reaction, but with \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) in the fourth NO CHANGE IS OBSERVED — it is not a strong enough reductant to reduce copper(II).
The inference is therefore about the relative oxidising strength of the two ions: \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) IS A STRONGER OXIDISING AGENT THAN \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\). A mild reductant such as an aldehyde is enough to reduce \(\text{Ag}^{+}\); only the much stronger \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2\) can reduce \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\). The chapter's Table 7.1 confirms it independently — \(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag} = 0.80\,\text{V}\) against \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu} = 0.34\,\text{V}\), and the more positive the potential the stronger the oxidant — as does the chapter's own observation that copper metal displaces silver from silver nitrate solution.
Answer: \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) is a stronger oxidising agent (more readily reduced) than \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\); this is why the weak reductant benzaldehyde reduces the first and not the second, while the strong reductant \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2\) reduces both.

In each case split the change into an oxidation half and a reduction half, balance atoms other than O and H, then balance O with water and H with \(\text{H}^{+}\) (adding \(\text{OH}^{-}\) to both sides afterwards for a basic medium), balance charge with electrons, scale the halves to a common number of electrons and add.
(a) BASIC. Oxidation: \(2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2\text{e}^{-}\). Reduction: \(\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{OH}^{-}\). Multiplying by 3 and 2 gives six electrons each way:
\(6\text{I}^{-}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{MnO}_4^{-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 3\text{I}_2\text{(s)} + 2\text{MnO}_2\text{(s)} + 8\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)}\)
(b) ACIDIC. Sulphur rises \(+4 \rightarrow +6\), manganese falls \(+7 \rightarrow +2\).
Oxidation: \(\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HSO}_4^{-} + 3\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-}\)
Reduction: \(\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 8\text{H}^{+} + 5\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Multiplying by 5 and 2 and cancelling the water and \(\text{H}^{+}\) common to both sides:
\(2\text{MnO}_4^{-}\text{(aq)} + 5\text{SO}_2\text{(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 5\text{HSO}_4^{-}\text{(aq)}\)
(c) ACIDIC. Iron rises \(+2 \rightarrow +3\), the peroxide oxygen falls \(-1 \rightarrow -2\).
Oxidation: \(\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-}\)  (taken twice)
Reduction: \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
\(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\text{(aq)} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)
(d) ACIDIC. Sulphur rises \(+4 \rightarrow +6\), chromium falls \(+6 \rightarrow +3\).
Oxidation: \(\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SO}_4^{2-} + 4\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-}\)  (taken three times)
Reduction: \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^{+} + 6\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Adding and cancelling:
\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 3\text{SO}_2\text{(g)} + 2\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + 3\text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)
Each of the four is balanced in atoms and in charge.

[Textbook misprint in part (a): the phosphorus product is printed \(\text{HPO}_2^{-}\), which puts phosphorus at \(+2\). The chapter's own equation 7.46 gives this species as the hypophosphite ion \(\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^{-}\), with phosphorus at \(+1\) — so the book contradicts itself between its text and this exercise. The equation below is balanced AS PRINTED, since that is the question set, and the book's own \(\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^{-}\) form is given alongside so a reader meeting either version can follow.] (a) \(\text{P}_4 + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{PH}_3 + \text{HPO}_2^{-}\). Phosphorus starts at \(0\); in \(\text{PH}_3\) it is \(-3\) and in \(\text{HPO}_2^{-}\) as printed it is \((+1) + x + 2(-2) = -1 \Rightarrow x = +2\). The same element is both raised and lowered, so this is a DISPROPORTIONATION and phosphorus is simultaneously the oxidising and the reducing agent.
Reduction half: \(\text{P}_4 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} + 12\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4\text{PH}_3 + 12\text{OH}^{-}\)
Oxidation half: \(\text{P}_4 + 12\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow 4\text{HPO}_2^{-} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} + 8\text{e}^{-}\)
Scaling to \(24\) electrons (\(\times 2\) and \(\times 3\)) and cancelling:
\(5\text{P}_4\text{(s)} + 12\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)} + 12\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 8\text{PH}_3\text{(g)} + 12\text{HPO}_2^{-}\text{(aq)}\)
By the oxidation-number method the same result follows directly: each phosphorus that is reduced drops by 3 and each that is oxidised rises by 2, so reduced and oxidised phosphorus must be in the ratio \(2 : 3\), giving 8 and 12 atoms out of the 20 in \(5\text{P}_4\).
It is worth noting that the chapter's own version of this reaction, equation 7.46, uses the hypophosphite ion \(\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^{-}\) (phosphorus at \(+1\)) rather than \(\text{HPO}_2^{-}\), and with that formula the balanced equation is the simpler \(\text{P}_4 + 3\text{OH}^{-} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{PH}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^{-}\).
(b) \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{ClO}_3^{-} \rightarrow \text{NO} + \text{Cl}^{-}\). Nitrogen rises \(-2 \rightarrow +2\) (four electrons per atom, eight per \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\)); chlorine falls \(+5 \rightarrow -1\) (six electrons). Balancing at the common multiple 24 electrons, three hydrazine to four chlorate:
Oxidation: \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NO} + 8\text{H}^{+} + 8\text{e}^{-}\)
Reduction: \(\text{ClO}_3^{-} + 6\text{H}^{+} + 6\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^{-} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
\(3\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\text{(l)} + 4\text{ClO}_3^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 6\text{NO(g)} + 4\text{Cl}^{-}\text{(aq)} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)
All the \(\text{H}^{+}\) cancels, so this equation is the same in acidic and in basic medium. Oxidising agent: \(\text{ClO}_3^{-}\). Reducing agent: \(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\).
(c) \(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{ClO}_2^{-} + \text{O}_2\). Chlorine falls \(+7 \rightarrow +3\) (four electrons per atom, eight per \(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7\)); the peroxide oxygen rises \(-1 \rightarrow 0\) (two electrons per \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\)), so one \(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7\) to four \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\).
Reduction: \(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} + 8\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{ClO}_2^{-} + 6\text{OH}^{-}\)
Oxidation: \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^{-}\)  (taken four times)
Adding and cancelling:
\(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\text{(aq)} + 2\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{ClO}_2^{-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 5\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)
Oxidising agent: \(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7\). Reducing agent: \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\). Note that in a basic medium no free \(\text{H}^{+}\) can survive, so the \(\text{H}^{+}\) printed among the products of the question is replaced here by hydroxide on the left and water on the right.
_note: Three points where the printed question and the printed chapter disagree with each other, all handled explicitly in the solution rather than silently corrected: (1) the exercise writes the phosphorus oxoanion as HPO2- (P at +2) whereas the chapter's own eq 7.46 writes H2PO2- (P at +1) — the solution balances the form the EXERCISE prints and gives the chapter's form alongside; (2) part (b) labels the chloride ion '(g)' where '(aq)' is meant; (3) part (c) shows H+ as a product although the instruction says basic medium. If the printed key balances (a) using H2PO2- it will not match our coefficients, and that is a difference of premise, not of arithmetic.

solution:
Assign oxidation numbers, treating the cyanide group as a unit in which nitrogen is \(-3\).
In cyanogen \((\text{CN})_2\) each carbon is bonded to a nitrogen and to the other carbon, so \(x + (-3) = 0\) per \(\text{CN}\) unit gives carbon \(= +3\).
In the cyanide ion \(\text{CN}^{-}\): \(x + (-3) = -1 \Rightarrow x = +2\).
In the cyanate ion \(\text{CNO}^{-}\): \(x + (-3) + (-2) = -1 \Rightarrow x = +4\).
From this several things follow.
1. It is a redox reaction, since oxidation numbers change.
2. More precisely it is a DISPROPORTIONATION: the carbon of cyanogen is simultaneously reduced (\(+3 \rightarrow +2\)) and oxidised (\(+3 \rightarrow +4\)). Cyanogen is thus both the oxidising and the reducing agent, and this is possible only because its carbon starts in an INTERMEDIATE state — the condition the chapter lays down for disproportionation.
3. The reaction has exactly the form of the chapter's alkaline halogen disproportionation, \(\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{ClO}^{-} + \text{Cl}^{-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), with \((\text{CN})_2\) in the place of \(\text{Cl}_2\), \(\text{CN}^{-}\) in the place of \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) and \(\text{CNO}^{-}\) in the place of \(\text{ClO}^{-}\). Cyanogen therefore behaves chemically like a halogen and is called a PSEUDOHALOGEN, the cyanide ion being the corresponding pseudohalide.
4. Like the halogen disproportionations of this chapter, it needs an alkaline medium.
Answer: the reaction tells us that cyanogen disproportionates in alkali — its carbon going to \(+2\) in cyanide and \(+4\) in cyanate from \(+3\) — and that \((\text{CN})_2\) is a pseudohalogen, behaving exactly as chlorine does with hydroxide.

Manganese starts at \(+3\) and ends in two different states: \(+2\) in \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) and \(+4\) in \(\text{MnO}_2\). This is a disproportionation, possible because \(+3\) is an intermediate state for manganese.
Reduction half: \(\text{Mn}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+}\)  (a gain of one electron)
Oxidation half: \(\text{Mn}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{H}^{+} + \text{e}^{-}\)  (a loss of one electron)
One electron is exchanged each way, so the two halves combine in a \(1 : 1\) ratio. Adding them and cancelling the electrons:
\(2\text{Mn}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{MnO}_2\text{(s)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}\)
Check: manganese \(2 = 2\); oxygen \(2 = 2\); hydrogen \(4 = 4\); charge \(+6\) on the left and \(+2 + 0 + 4 = +6\) on the right. Balanced.

(a) ONLY NEGATIVE: FLUORINE. It is the most electronegative element there is, so in any bond it forms the shared pair belongs entirely to it. The chapter states the consequence outright — in all its compounds fluorine has an oxidation number of \(-1\) — and it can never be assigned a positive value.
(b) ONLY POSITIVE: CAESIUM. It is an alkali metal, and by the chapter's rule all alkali metals have an oxidation number of \(+1\) in their compounds. Being one of the most electropositive elements it always gives its single valence electron away and never takes electrons from anything, so no negative state arises.
(c) BOTH POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE: IODINE. It is \(-1\) in the iodides, where it is the more electronegative partner (as in \(\text{KI}\)), and positive when combined with the still more electronegative oxygen — the chapter notes that chlorine, bromine and iodine have positive oxidation numbers in oxoacids and oxoanions, for example \(+5\) in \(\text{IO}_3^{-}\).
(d) NEITHER: NEON. It is a noble gas with a complete octet, forms no compounds, and so is met only in the free state, where by the chapter's first rule its oxidation number is zero — neither positive nor negative.
Answers: (a) F  (b) Cs  (c) I  (d) Ne.

Chlorine is the oxidising agent here, falling from \(0\) in \(\text{Cl}_2\) to \(-1\) in chloride, and sulphur dioxide is the reducing agent, its sulphur rising from \(+4\) to \(+6\). Since the change happens in water, the water supplies the oxygen the sulphur needs.
Oxidation half: \(\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SO}_4^{2-} + 4\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-}\)
Reduction half: \(\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^{-}\)
Two electrons are exchanged each way, so the halves add directly:
\(\text{Cl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{SO}_2\text{(aq)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^{-}\text{(aq)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}\)
Written in molecular form the same change is
\(\text{Cl}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{HCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)
Check: chlorine \(2 = 2\), sulphur \(1 = 1\), oxygen \(2 + 2 = 4\), hydrogen \(4 = 2 + 2\). Balanced.
The harmful free chlorine is thereby converted to harmless chloride ion, which is why sulphur dioxide is used as the dechlorinating agent.

The chapter's condition for disproportionation is that the element must be able to exist in AT LEAST THREE oxidation states and must start in an INTERMEDIATE one, so that it can go both up and down.
(a) NON-METALS. Four elements meet the condition, and the chapter itself gives the reaction for each:
Phosphorus, going from \(0\) down to \(-3\) and up to \(+1\):
\(\text{P}_4 + 3\text{OH}^{-} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{PH}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^{-}\)
Sulphur, going from \(0\) down to \(-2\) and up to \(+2\):
\(\text{S}_8 + 12\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow 4\text{S}^{2-} + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Chlorine (and likewise bromine and iodine), going from \(0\) down to \(-1\) and up to \(+1\):
\(\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{ClO}^{-} + \text{Cl}^{-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Oxygen, in hydrogen peroxide, going from \(-1\) down to \(-2\) and up to \(0\):
\(2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2\)
FLUORINE IS THE ONE NON-METAL THAT CANNOT. The chapter says so explicitly: being the most electronegative element it cannot exhibit any positive oxidation state, so it has no state above \(0\) to disproportionate into and shows no disproportionation tendency.
(b) METALS. Any metal with three accessible oxidation states, taken in an intermediate one, will do. Three examples:
Copper, \(\text{Cu(I)}\) lying between \(0\) and \(+2\):
\(2\text{Cu}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{Cu}\)
Manganese, \(\text{Mn(III)}\) lying between \(+2\) and \(+4\):
\(2\text{Mn}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + \text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{H}^{+}\)
Mercury, \(\text{Hg(I)}\) lying between \(0\) and \(+2\):
\(\text{Hg}_2^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Hg}^{2+} + \text{Hg}\)
Gold, \(\text{Au(I)}\) lying between \(0\) and \(+3\), is a fourth: \(3\text{Au}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2\text{Au}\).
That each of these metals really does have three states is visible in the chapter itself, which writes \(\text{Cu(I)I}\) beside \(\text{Cu(II)O}\), \(\text{Mn(II)O}\) beside \(\text{Mn(IV)O}_2\), \(\text{Au(I)Cl}\) beside \(\text{Au(III)Cl}_3\), and \(\text{Hg}_2\text{(I)Cl}_2\) as the reduced form of \(\text{Hg(II)Cl}_2\).
_note: The chapter supplies the four non-metal disproportionations of part (a) verbatim (eqs 7.45-7.48) and states the fluorine exception explicitly. It gives NO metal disproportionation reaction anywhere; the three in part (b) are supplied from outside the chapter, although the multiple oxidation states they rest on (Cu I/II, Mn II/IV, Au I/III, Hg I/II) are all printed in the chapter's own Problem 7.3.

solution:
The first step of the Ostwald process is the catalytic oxidation of ammonia:
\(4\text{NH}_3\text{(g)} + 5\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow 4\text{NO(g)} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}\)
(Nitrogen rises from \(-3\) to \(+2\) and oxygen falls from \(0\) to \(-2\), so this is a redox change; ammonia is the reductant and dioxygen the oxidant.)
Molar masses: \(\text{NH}_3 = 14 + 3(1) = 17\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(\text{O}_2 = 2(16) = 32\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(\text{NO} = 14 + 16 = 30\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Moles supplied:
\(n(\text{NH}_3) = \dfrac{10.00}{17} = 0.5882\,\text{mol}\)
\(n(\text{O}_2) = \dfrac{20.00}{32} = 0.6250\,\text{mol}\)
Identify the limiting reagent. The equation needs \(\text{NH}_3\) and \(\text{O}_2\) in the ratio \(4 : 5\), so \(0.5882\,\text{mol}\) of ammonia would require
\(0.5882 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 0.7353\,\text{mol}\) of dioxygen,
but only \(0.6250\,\text{mol}\) is available. DIOXYGEN IS THEREFORE THE LIMITING REAGENT and it alone fixes the yield.
From the equation, \(5\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) give \(4\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{NO}\):
\(n(\text{NO}) = 0.6250 \times \dfrac{4}{5} = 0.5000\,\text{mol}\)
\(m(\text{NO}) = 0.5000 \times 30 = 15.00\,\text{g}\)
(Only \(0.5000\,\text{mol} = 8.50\,\text{g}\) of the ammonia is consumed, so \(1.50\,\text{g}\) of it is left over.)
Maximum weight of nitric oxide obtainable \(= 15.00\,\text{g}\).

The table is attached to this question so it can be answered without hunting for it.] A redox reaction between two couples is feasible when the couple acting as the OXIDANT has the more positive standard electrode potential, so that the overall cell potential \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}(\text{reduced species}) - E^{\ominus}(\text{oxidised species})\) comes out positive.
From the chapter's table of standard electrode potentials: \(\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^{-} = 1.09\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag} = 0.80\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+} = 0.77\,\text{V}\), \(\text{I}_2/\text{I}^{-} = 0.54\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu} = 0.34\,\text{V}\).
(a) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{I}^{-}\): \(0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23\,\text{V}\). FEASIBLE — \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) oxidises iodide:
\(2\text{Fe}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{I}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{I}_2\text{(s)}\)
(b) \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) and \(\text{Cu}\): \(0.80 - 0.34 = +0.46\,\text{V}\). FEASIBLE:
\(2\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\)
(c) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Cu}\): \(0.77 - 0.34 = +0.43\,\text{V}\). FEASIBLE:
\(2\text{Fe}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\)
(d) \(\text{Ag(s)}\) and \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\): here \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) would have to oxidise silver metal, giving \(0.77 - 0.80 = -0.03\,\text{V}\). NOT FEASIBLE — silver is the weaker reducing agent of the two, so the reaction does not go in this direction.
(e) \(\text{Br}_2\) and \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\): \(1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32\,\text{V}\). FEASIBLE — bromine oxidises iron(II):
\(\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^{-}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+}\text{(aq)}\)
Answer: (a), (b), (c) and (e) are feasible; (d) is not.

solution:
Two rules settle each case. At the CATHODE the species with the highest reduction potential is reduced; at the ANODE the species most easily oxidised (lowest reduction potential) is oxidised — and if the anode is made of an ACTIVE metal it dissolves in preference to anything in the solution. Note also that neither \(\text{NO}_3^{-}\) nor \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) can be oxidised, because nitrogen and sulphur in them are already at their maximum oxidation states \(+5\) and \(+6\).
(i) \(\text{AgNO}_3\)(aq) with SILVER electrodes. Cathode: \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) is reduced (\(E^{\ominus} = 0.80\,\text{V}\), far above water's), so silver is deposited — \(\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag(s)}\). Anode: the silver electrode is itself the most easily oxidised species present and dissolves — \(\text{Ag(s)} \rightarrow \text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{e}^{-}\). Net effect: silver simply transfers from the anode to the cathode and the concentration of the solution is unchanged. This is the basis of silver plating and electro-refining.
(ii) \(\text{AgNO}_3\)(aq) with PLATINUM electrodes. Cathode: silver is deposited as before. Anode: platinum is inert and cannot dissolve, and nitrate cannot be oxidised, so water is oxidised — \(2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{e}^{-}\). Dioxygen is evolved at the anode and the solution turns acidic.
(iii) DILUTE \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) with PLATINUM electrodes. Cathode: \(2\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{(g)}\) — dihydrogen. Anode: sulphate cannot be oxidised, so water is — \(2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{e}^{-}\) — giving dioxygen. The overall result is the electrolysis of water, with hydrogen and oxygen evolved in the volume ratio \(2 : 1\).
(iv) \(\text{CuCl}_2\)(aq) with PLATINUM electrodes. Cathode: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu(s)}\) (\(E^{\ominus} = 0.34\,\text{V}\), well above the potential for reducing water), so copper is deposited. Anode: \(2\text{Cl}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} + 2\text{e}^{-}\) — chlorine is evolved. On the standard potentials alone the oxidation of water (\(1.23\,\text{V}\)) is very slightly easier than that of chloride (\(1.36\,\text{V}\)), but in practice chlorine is discharged because oxygen evolution on platinum is kinetically hindered.
Answers: (i) Ag deposited at the cathode, the silver anode dissolves; (ii) Ag deposited, \(\text{O}_2\) evolved; (iii) \(\text{H}_2\) evolved, \(\text{O}_2\) evolved; (iv) Cu deposited, \(\text{Cl}_2\) evolved.
_note: This chapter does not teach electrolysis. Section 7.4 develops the redox couple, the Daniell cell and the standard electrode potential, and then says outright that electrode reactions and cells are studied in Class XII. The answers above are reasoned from the electrode-potential ordering the chapter DOES give (Table 7.1) plus the standard convention that an active anode dissolves; the overpotential remark in (iv) comes from outside the chapter entirely and is flagged as such in the answer.

solution:
A metal displaces another metal from a solution of its salt when it is the better reducing agent, i.e. when it gives up electrons more readily. On the chapter's scale that means the more NEGATIVE standard electrode potential wins, and the values it tabulates are
\(\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg} = -2.36\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al} = -1.66\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn} = -0.76\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe} = -0.44\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu} = +0.34\,\text{V}\).
Reading them from the most negative down gives the order in which each metal displaces those that follow it:
\(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\)
So magnesium displaces aluminium, zinc, iron and copper from their salt solutions; aluminium displaces zinc, iron and copper; zinc displaces iron and copper; iron displaces copper; and copper displaces none of them. The chapter's own example is the last step but one,
\(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\)
Answer: \(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\), each metal displacing every metal to its right.

The chapter states the rule directly: a NEGATIVE standard electrode potential means the couple is a stronger reducing agent than the \(\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2\) couple, and a POSITIVE one means it is weaker. So reducing power increases as the potential becomes more negative.
List the given values in order from the most positive to the most negative:
\(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag} = 0.80\,\text{V}\)
\(\text{Hg}^{2+}/\text{Hg} = 0.79\,\text{V}\)
\(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr} = -0.74\,\text{V}\)
\(\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg} = -2.37\,\text{V}\)
\(\text{K}^{+}/\text{K} = -2.93\,\text{V}\)
Reading that list from top to bottom is reading reducing power from weakest to strongest.
Increasing order of reducing power: \(\text{Ag} < \text{Hg} < \text{Cr} < \text{Mg} < \text{K}\).
Potassium is the strongest reducing agent of the five and silver the weakest.

Split the reaction into its two half reactions and put each in its own beaker, joining the solutions by a salt bridge and the metals by a wire, exactly as in the chapter's Daniell cell. Zinc is oxidised, so the zinc rod in zinc sulphate solution is the anode; silver ion is reduced, so the silver rod in silver nitrate solution is the cathode. Writing the oxidised form before the reduced one and the anode on the left, the cell is
\(\text{Zn(s)} \mid \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} \mid \text{Ag(s)}\)
(i) NEGATIVELY CHARGED ELECTRODE: the ZINC electrode. Zinc atoms are oxidised there and push electrons into the external wire, so the zinc rod accumulates negative charge and is the negative terminal — this is the anode, marked with a minus sign in the chapter's own diagram of the Daniell cell.
(ii) CARRIERS OF THE CURRENT: outside the cell, in the metallic wire, the carriers are ELECTRONS, travelling from the zinc electrode to the silver electrode. Inside the cell the electrons do not travel at all; the circuit is completed by IONS migrating through the two solutions and the salt bridge, cations moving towards the silver (cathode) compartment and anions towards the zinc (anode) compartment. Note that the conventional current direction is opposite to that of the electron flow.
(iii) INDIVIDUAL ELECTRODE REACTIONS:
At the anode (oxidation): \(\text{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-}\)
At the cathode (reduction): \(2\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag(s)}\)
Adding the two gives back the overall cell reaction, \(\text{Zn(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}\).
Using the chapter's tabulated potentials, \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = +1.56\,\text{V}\); the positive value confirms that the reaction runs spontaneously in the direction written, so the cell delivers current.
